courses.description: This experiential course teaches the art of practicing psychological well-being based on principles from Eastern and Western philosophies (e.g., mindfulness, positive psychology, cognitive therapy, and neuroscience) within cognitive science. Each week, there is a short lecture on a given topic combined with workshop-style exercises.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Undergraduate Seminar
courses.description: Special topics in cognitive science are discussed. P/NP grades only. (May be repeated when topics vary.)

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Independent Study
courses.description: Independent literature or laboratory research by arrangement with and under direction of a Department of Cognitive Science faculty member.
courses.prerequisites_text: lower-division standing, completion of thirty units of UC San Diego undergraduate study, a minimum UC San Diego GPA of 3.0, and a completed and approved Special Studies form.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Cyborgs Now and in the Future
courses.description: Covers the theories of situated, distributed, enactive, and embodied cognition. Explains how cyborgs are a natural consequence of our current understanding of embodied minds embedded in culturally shaped niches; how mental systems can be distributed over other people and things.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 1 or COGS 10.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Sensation and Perception
courses.description: An introduction to the experimental study of cognition with a focus on sensation and perception.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 1.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Learning, Memory, and Attention
courses.description: A survey of the experimental study of learning, memory, and attention. Topics include conditioning, automaticity, divided attention, memory systems, and the nature of mental representation.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 1. Recommended: COGS 101A.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Language
courses.description: An introduction to structure of natural language, and to the cognitive processes that underline its acquisition, comprehension, and production. This course covers findings from linguistics, computer science, psychology, and cognitive neuroscience to provide an integrated perspective on human language abilities. Prerequisites : COGS 1 and 14A.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Cognitive Design Studio
courses.description: This project-based course focuses on learning and applying the process of human-centered cognitive design. Students work in teams to design and evaluate a prototype application or redesign an existing system. Emphasizes contextual inquiry, user research, ideation, iterative design, and evaluation.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 102B.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Neuroanatomy and Physiology
courses.description: This first course in the sequence focuses on principles of brain organization, from neurons to circuits to functional networks. It explores developmental plasticity, neuronal connectivity, cellular communication, complex signaling, and how these various dimensions form functional brain systems.
courses.prerequisites_text: BILD 12 or COGS 17.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Systems Neuroscience
courses.description: This course focuses on the electrical dynamics of neurons and how their patterns relate to perception, thought, and action. Neural activity patterns underlying vision, touch, audition, proprioception, and head orientation are examined in detail. Also examined are motor control, sleep/wake state production, action planning, learning, memory, attention, spatial cognition and function of the cerebellum, basal ganglia, and hippocampus.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 107A.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Cognitive Neuroscience
courses.description: This course reviews research investigating the neural bases for human mental processes, including processing of affective, social, linguistic, and visuospatial information, as well as memory, attention, and executive functions. Also discussed are brain development and brain aging, and the nature of intelligence and creativity.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 107B and its prerequisites.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Data Science in Practice
courses.description: Data science is multidisciplinary, covering computer science, statistics, cognitive science and psychology, data visualization, artificial intelligence and machine learning, among others. This course teaches critical skills needed to pursue a data science career using hands-on programming and experimental challenges.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 11 or CSE 8A or COGS 18 or DSC 10 or MAE 8.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Modeling and Data Analysis
courses.description: Exposure to the basic computational methods useful throughout cognitive science. Computing basic statistics, modeling learning individuals, evolving populations, communicating agents, and corpus-based linguistics will be considered.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 14B, MATH 18 or MATH 31AH, and COGS 18 or CSE 7 or CSE 8A or CSE 11.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Humor
courses.description: In this course we will explore the psychology, philosophy, and evolutionary origins of humor and laughter.
courses.prerequisites_text: upper-division standing.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Growing Minds: Babies, Brains, and Machines
courses.description: What would it take to build a robot that could learn like a human infant? This course explores the science of learning in natural and artificial minds. What comes easily to babies but is hard for machines, and vice versa? The course will explore connections between infant development, cognitive neuroscience, and advances in AI to understand how natural and artificial minds grow across topics such as perception, motor development, language, curiosity, and social cognition.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 1.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Computational Modeling and Analysis of Human Behavior
courses.description: Behavioral data is everywhere and reveals how we think, learn, and act. This course equips you to analyze, model, and predict behavior using tools from machine learning. We will explore a variety of computational models, including Bayesian models, latent variable models, and time series analysis, and apply them to real-world datasets. A practical course for students interested in behavioral data science or computational research in human behavior.
courses.prerequisites_text: MATH 18 or MATH 31AH and MATH 180A or MATH 183 or MATH 186 or ECE 109 or ECON 120A or MAE 108 and COGS 108 or COGS 109 or COGS 118A or COGS 118B or COGS 188 or CSE 150A or CSE 151A or CSE 158 or CSE 158R or DSC 148 or ECE 174 or ECE 175A.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Advanced Interaction Design
courses.description: This is a studio class for students who are passionate about diving deep into interaction design and honing their design skills. Introduces social computing, input and interaction techniques, and information design. Students will regularly present work in a studio format.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 11 or 8B and COGS 120 or CSE 170.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Thinking with Computers
courses.description: This course surveys the field of human-computer interaction and the ideas and technologies that have shaped its development.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 120 or COGS 121 or CSE 170.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Data-Driven UX/Product Design
courses.description: Create a UX/product design case study for your portfolio; team project with user research, data science, prototyping, and user testing. Prerequisites : VIS 41 or VIS 30 or DSGN 1 or COGS 1.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Neural Data Science
courses.description: Project-based course in which students will use computational notebooks to perform exploratory data analyses and to test hypotheses in large neuroscience datasets, including the differences between unique neuron types, leveraging text mining of the neuroscience literature, and human neuroimaging analyses.
courses.prerequisites_text: BILD 62 or COGS 18 or CSE 6R or CSE 8A and COGS 118C or COGS 189 or DSC 120 or ECE 45 or MATH 144.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Music and the Mind
courses.description: Explores how humans (and other species) process music, including pitch, meter, emotion, motor aspects, links to language, brain activity. Students should have experience reading musical notation.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 101A or COGS 101B or COGS 101C.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Upper-Division Seminar on Special Topics
courses.description: Special topics in cognitive science are discussed. (May be repeated when topics vary.)
courses.prerequisites_text: department approval.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Mirror Neuron System
courses.description: This class will examine the neuroanatomy, physiology, and functional correlates of the human mirror neuron system and its putative role in social cognition, e.g., action understanding, empathy, and theory of mind. We will examine the developmental, neuroimaging, electrophysiological, as well as clinical evidence, for and against this hypothesis.
courses.prerequisites_text: upper-division standing.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Brain Disorders and Cognition
courses.description: A review of the patterns of impaired and intact cognitive abilities present in brain-damaged patients in terms of damage to one or more components of a model of normal cognitive functioning.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 107A.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Modeling the Evolution of Cognition
courses.description: This interdisciplinary course integrates data on evolutionary theory, hominid prehistory, primate behavior, comparative neuroanatomy, cognitive development, and collaboration. After lectures, readings, and discussion of the literature, students generate a detailed timeline of five million years of human cognitive evolution. Students may not receive credit for COGS 184 and COGS 184GS.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 17 or COGS 107A or COGS 107B or COGS 107C or BILD 12.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Usability and Information Architecture
courses.description: Examines the cognitive basis of successful web and multimedia design. Topics: information architecture, navigation, usability, graphic layout, transaction design, and how to understand user interaction.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 18 or CSE 11 or CSE 8A and COGS 10 or DSGN 1.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Practicum in Professional Web Design
courses.description: This course follows up on the basics of multimedia design taught in COGS 187A. Students will probe more deeply into selective topics, such as animation, navigation, graphical display of information, and narrative coherence.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 187A or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Honors Thesis in Cognitive Science
courses.description: This course will provide honors candidates an opportunity to complete the research on and preparation of an honors thesis under close faculty supervision. Oral presentation of student’s thesis is required to receive honors; additionally, student must receive grade of A– or better in 190B and 190C to receive honors. See “ Cognitive Science Honors Program ” section for more information.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 190B with grade of A– or better and formal admittance to the Cognitive Science Honors Program.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Preparation for Thesis Presentation
courses.description: This course is affiliated with the honors program (190A-B-C) and is required of honors students during spring quarter. Its aim is to prepare students to present research results to an audience. Emphasis will be on the oral presentation (organization, wording, graphics), but there will also be some discussion about written research reports. Seminar style format with occasional short lectures wherein students will practice oral presentations and provide constructive criticism to each other.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 190A-B and COGS 198.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Pedagogy and Learning Apprenticeship
courses.description: Under the supervision of an instructor, undergraduate students gain teaching experience through practical experiences in course management and effective teaching methods. P/NP grades only. May be taken for credit two times.
courses.prerequisites_text: upper-division standing; 3.0 GPA; instructor and department approval.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Cognitive Science Internship
courses.description: The student will undertake a program of practical research in a supervised work environment. Topics to be researched may vary, but in each case the course will provide skills for carrying out these studies. P/NP grades only. May be taken for credit up to three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: upper-division standing; 2.5 GPA; department approval.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Special Project
courses.description: This independent study course is for individual, advanced students who wish to complete a one-quarter reading or research project under the mentorship of a faculty member. Students should contact faculty whose research interests them to discuss possible projects. P/NP grades only. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: upper-division standing; 2.5 GPA; consent of instructor and department approval.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Computational Modeling of Cognition
courses.description: This course surveys some key methods of computational modeling across a range of cognitive science fields. Bringing together basic tools of probabilistic modeling, information theory, machine learning, and computational neuroscience. Students presumed to be facile with probability, statistics, linear algebra, calculus.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Introduction to Thesis Research
courses.description: This course is taken to focus the students’ development of a thesis topic and research proposal. Students prepare an outline of thesis proposal and make an oral public presentation of the proposed topic prior to the end of the third year. S/U only.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Statistical Machine Learning for Social Sciences
courses.description: Advanced methods and fundamental principles for learning from data. Emphasis is on foundational methods in supervised and unsupervised machine learning problems, covering trade-offs inherent in model design, training, evaluation, selection, and validation. Students will not receive credit for both COGS 209 and CSS 206. Recommended preparation: introductory statistics and familiarity with scientific programming and analysis software (MATLAB, Python, or R).
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Introduction to Research
courses.description: This sequence is an intensive research project. Students under faculty mentorship perform a thorough analysis of the problem and the literature, carry out original studies, and prepare oral and written presentations. Students should aim for a report of publishable quality. Letter grade required.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Research Methods in Cognitive Science
courses.description: Issues in design, implementation, and evaluation of research in cognitive science are discussed. Students will present and comment on their own research projects in progress. Discussions also include presentations of research to various audiences, abstracts, reviews, grant process, and scientific ethics. Letter grade required.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Design at Large
courses.description: (Cross-listed with DSGN 219 and CSE 219.) New societal challenges, cultural values, and technological opportunities are changing design, and vice versa. The seminar explores this increased scale, real-world engagement, and disruptive impact. Invited speakers from UC San Diego and beyond share cutting-edge research on interaction, design, and learning. S/U grades only. May be taken for credit up to eighteen times. Students may receive a combined total of eighteen units for COGS 229, CSE 219, and DSGN 219.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Seminar on Special Topics
courses.description: Specific topics in cognitive science are discussed. (May be repeated when topics vary.)

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Genetics and Individuality
courses.description: Evidence for the heritability and for the association of genetic variants with behavioral and neural phenotypes will be reviewed. Integrative models of gene-environment interaction will be discussed. Guest faculty will describe their own work in this area.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Cognitive Science Laboratory Rotation
courses.description: Laboratory rotations provide students with experience in the various experimental methods used in cognitive science.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor. S/U only.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Introduction to Communication
courses.description: This course is an introduction to the history, theory, and practice of communication. Topics covered include language literacy, representation, semiotics, mediated technologies, institutional formations, and social interaction. Course work may involve media production (for example, writing, video and media production, or performance). No credit for COMM 10 if taken after COMM 10R.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Digital Media Literacy: Analyzing Forms, Practices, and Infrastructures of Mediated Public Life
courses.description: The role of digital communication in a democratic system, and the ways mass media both facilitate and inhibit the development of a viable public sphere. By exploring today’s digital communication dynamics, students will have the opportunity to become more mindful, active consumers of media and to feel empowered to be engaged participants in public life.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Introduction to Promotional Communication
courses.description: A critical-cultural communication introduction to fields of practice that publicize, promote, or increase awareness of brands, ideas, products, and causes. Exploration of public communication industries and practices, the pressures that shape these industries and practices, and their implications for culture and society. Course will address major promotional industries such as advertising, public relations, marketing, and social media.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Presenting and Public Speaking
courses.description: This course covers the basics of communication in public and professional settings. Students will cultivate their own speaking style while developing skills in delivery, performance, and persuasion. They will learn how to create a slide deck as well as prepare for speeches, interviews, and Q and As.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Topics in Communication
courses.description: Introductory study in the discipline of communication, covering foundational skills and topics in areas like culture, technology, science communication, activism, and the environment. Topic and description are determined by the instructor and provided by the department quarterly.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Public Presentation and Persuasion—Speech and Debate
courses.description: Throughout history, important advances in a democratic society have emerged most often from civil, rigorous discussion, debate, and persuasion. Students develop research, critical thinking, presentation, public speaking, and argumentation skills through in-class practice speeches and debates, along with participation in intercollegiate speech and debate tournaments. May be taken for credit up to six times.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: First-year Student Seminar
courses.description: The First-year Student Seminar Program is designed to provide new students with the opportunity to explore an intellectual topic with a faculty member in a small seminar setting. First-year student seminars are offered in all campus departments and undergraduate colleges, and topics vary from quarter to quarter. Enrollment is limited to fifteen to twenty students, with preference given to entering first-year students.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Communication, Culture, and Representation
courses.description: This course is a critical introduction to the history of representation, surveying a range of theories and methods that have been used to understand and shape representational practices. The course will focus on relationships between form and content across various representational genres in shifting cultural contexts. Course work may integrate scholarly study with production (e.g., image-making or video/media production). No credit for COMM 100BR if taken after COMM 100B.
courses.prerequisites_text: junior or senior standing.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Introduction to Audiovisual Media Practices
courses.description: This upper-division course is required as the gateway to all future communication media production courses. Students will learn about contemporary media practices such as film, video, digital/online, and social media production, and how these practices are formed by technical and social constraints. In the studio portion of this course, students will work hands-on with video and new media equipment to apply what they have learned.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Production of Activist Media
courses.description: In this course, we ask what techniques, strategies, and platforms we might engage to present messages in an impactful and ethical way. We engage with different media forms each quarter, maintaining an emphasis on production and documentary storytelling. The aim of this class is to demystify the idea of a “media activist” by guiding students through the development of their own media activism.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 or COMM 20 or COMM 30 or COMM 30GS or COMM 40 and COMM 101.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: MPL: Documentary Sketchbook
courses.description: Digital video is the medium used in this class both as a production technology and as a device to explore the theory and practice of documentary production. Technical demonstrations, lectures, production exercises, and readings will emphasize the interrelation between production values and ethics, problems of representation, and documentary history. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and COMM 101.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: MMPP: Practicum in New Media and Community Life
courses.description: A combined lecture/lab in a specially designed after-school setting in southeastern San Diego working with children and adults. Students design new media and produce special projects, and explore issues related to human development, social justice, and community life. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: none

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: MMPP: Studio Television
courses.description: This course offers students the opportunity to produce and engage in critical discussions around various television production formats. We will study and produce a variety of projects, including public service announcements, panel programs, scripted drama, and performance productions. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and COMM 101 or VIS 70N.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: CM: Documentary History and Theory
courses.description: History of nonfiction film and video. Through film and written texts, we survey the nonfiction film genre, considering technological innovations, ethical issues, and formal movements related to these representations of the “real.”
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Data and AI Industries
courses.description: Advances in AI and data science raise new and old issues about the role data plays in society. Students will learn how institutions (especially cultural industries) collect data, make predictions, and automate labor. Students will critically engage with data/AI practices and cultural representations of data/AI, discussing issues like privacy, power, bias, representation, regulation, and labor. Students will learn high-level tech concepts, but this class has no programming requirement.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10, COMM 20, COMM 30, COMM 30GS, or COMM 40.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: CI: Tourism: Global Industry and Cultural Form
courses.description: The largest industry in the world has far-reaching cultural ramifications. We will explore tourism’s history and its contemporary cultural effects, taking the perspective of the “toured” as well as that of the tourist.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Advertising and Society
courses.description: Advertising as a commercial and social force. The development of advertising, branding, and consumer culture in the United States; the history and political economy of advertising in mass and digital media; semiotics and representation in advertisements; influencers, authenticity, and the monetization of self and community; subversion and rebellion within systems of advertisement and promotion.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10, COMM 20, COMM 30, COMM 30GS, or COMM 40.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: TV Industry
courses.description: This course asks how visual images contribute to our understanding of the world and ourselves. The course will apply theoretical approaches from media studies, art history, gender studies, and social theory to analyze cultures of science, art, mass media, and everyday life. No credit for COMM 106V if taken after COMM 106VR.
courses.prerequisites_text: junior or senior standing.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Politics of Bodies: Gender and Biomedicine
courses.description: This course explores the construction of gender by biomedicine, and the influence of conceptions of gender on the development of biomedicine. From challenges to binary conceptions of sex to the intersection of race and pharmaceutical development around the world, the course will examine the ways in which embodied experiences of gender, sexuality, and race have interacted with social processes of biomedicalization and pharmaceuticalization.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: MC: Propaganda and Persuasion
courses.description: Propaganda, in political-economic, national settings; Soviet Union; Nazi Germany; US World War I and II. Propaganda films, contribution of filmmakers to propaganda campaign. Explore issues in propaganda; persuasive communication; political propaganda; persuasive advertising; public relations; practical, ethical perspectives.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: CSI: Human Rights, Communication, and Contemporary Global Justice
courses.description: How should we as global citizens respond to the horrifying human rights abuses that saturate news headlines and social media posts? How do communication practices, the right to information, freedom of expression, and media and journalists function within the contemporary human rights regime? Examine human rights protections—against genocide, torture, enslavement, political persecution, gender violence, and climate displacement—and their violation through case studies from 1945 to the present.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: CSI: Public History and Museum Studies
courses.description: This course will explore the role that “public history”—history as created for general audiences—plays in communicating cultural and national identities by examining museum exhibitions, their controversies, and how material objects mediate interpretations of the past.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Action Cinema
courses.description: This course traces the history of the action film genre with particular attention to its historical contexts, its social meanings, and its longstanding popularity with audiences. Topics and issues to be covered will include early cinema and serial queens; genre and the action film as hybrid; the aesthetics of action; the 1980s and the blockbuster; action cinema and gender; the rise of the franchise and transnational cinema.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10, COMM 20, COMM 30, COMM 30GS, or COMM 40.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Advanced Persuasion
courses.description: This course instructs advanced strategies, tactics, and presentation skills necessary for superior performance in intercollegiate speech and debate competitions. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 80.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Media Audiences
courses.description: Examines the complex relationship between mass media and the consumers and viewers they target. This course covers theories about audiences, reading practices of audiences, the economics of audiences, and the role of audiences in the digital era.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Science Fiction
courses.description: This course focuses on science fiction’s critical investigation of history, identity, and society across a range of media forms, including film, television, and literature. No credit for COMM 143 if taken after COMM 143R.
courses.prerequisites_text: junior or senior standing.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Southern California in Cinema
courses.description: This class examines the history and representation of Southern California on film. Consider the emergence of Hollywood as a defining moment in the history of Los Angeles and how film is central to the popular imagination of social life in Southern California. Examine the cinematic representation of different communities and neighborhoods and discuss topics such as car culture and regional sprawl, the beach as imagined lifestyle, and noir as regional critique.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 100A, COMM 100B, or COMM 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Latinx Space, Place, and Culture
courses.description: This diversity, equity, and inclusion course requirement approved course explores the power of place in the formation and representation of Latinx identities and communities in Southern California. It highlights past and current struggles to recuperate and sustain a sense of place for marginalized and displaced peoples against the colonization and racialization of formerly indigenous and Mexican territory. Students conduct research in various locations at the center of the cultural politics of Latinx place-making.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Bilingual Communication
courses.description: This course is designed to introduce students to multiple settings where bilingualism is the mode of communication. Examination of how such settings are socially constructed and culturally based. Language policy, bilingual education, and linguistic minorities, as well as field activities included.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Communication and Social Machines
courses.description: An examination of the questions that developments in robotics pose to the scholars of communication: How do we communicate when our interlocutors are nonhumans? How do we study objects that are claimed to be endowed with social and affective character?
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Culture, Domination, and Resistance
courses.description: Explores theories and narratives of cultural power, contemporary practices of resistance. Texts from a wide range of disciplines consider how domination is enacted, enforced, and what modes of resistance are employed to contend with uses and abuses of political power.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Advanced Studies in Communication Theory
courses.description: How are messages created, transmitted, and received? What is the relationship between thinking and communicating? How are linguistic processes embedded in sociocultural practices? Course discusses classic texts in the field of communication theory stemming from linguistics, semiotics, philosophy of language, literary theory.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Citizen Consumers
courses.description: This course considers the idea of the citizen-consumer that organizes much of contemporary urban planning and processes of identity, class, race, and gender formation in cities globally. Focusing on contemporary service oriented economies, we will critically explore how consumption spaces, such as shopping malls, theme parks, plazas, markets, parks, beaches, and tourist resorts, are critical nodes to understand neoliberal patterns of land transformation, labor exploitation, and social change.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Junior Seminar in Communication
courses.description: The junior seminar enables a detailed examination of a specific topic from the field of communication selected by the instructor, exploring in greater depth theories and methods introduced in the core communication curriculum. Seminars are limited to thirty students with a heavy focus on class participation. Students complete a research project with a significant final product (typically a research paper). No credit for COMM 190 if taken after COMM 190R.
courses.prerequisites_text: junior or senior standing and COMM 10 and at least one from COMM 100A-B-C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Research Seminar in Washington, D.C.
courses.description: (Same as POLI 194, USP 194, HITO 193, SOCI 194, and COGS 194) Course attached to six-unit internship taken by students participating in the UCDC program. Involves weekly seminar meetings with faculty and teaching assistants and a substantial research paper.
courses.prerequisites_text: participation in UCDC program.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Directed Group Study in Communication
courses.description: Directed group study on a topic or in a field not included in the regular curriculum by special arrangement with a faculty member. May be taken three times for credit.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor. (P/NP grades only.)

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Independent Study in Communication
courses.description: Independent study and research under the direction of a member of the faculty. May be taken three times for credit.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor. (P/NP grades only.)

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Honors Project Completion
courses.description: Under the guidance of both Honors Seminar director and faculty mentor, students will complete their thesis or media production and prepare for a presentation of their finished product at a public event sponsored by the department.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 196A-B and consent of instructor. (P/NP grades only.)

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Historical Methods for Communication Research
courses.description: Different approaches to conducting historical research in communication. Such approaches may include the social history of communication technology; structuralist and poststructuralist accounts of language, media, and collective memory; and new historicist treatments of cultural history. Sources, documentation, and the nature of argument from historical evidence are emphasized.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Seminar in Science Studies
courses.description: Study and discussion of a selected topic in the science studies field with an emphasis on the development of research and writing skills. The topic varies from year to year.
courses.prerequisites_text: enrollment in the Science Studies Program or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Colloquium in Science Studies
courses.description: A forum for the presentation and discussion of research in progress in science studies by graduate students, faculty, and visitors. Students must attend the colloquium series for their entire first and second years. They receive course credit in one quarter each year.
courses.prerequisites_text: enrollment in the Science Studies Program.

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Geographies of Difference, Exclusion and Conflict
courses.description: This seminar focuses on how differences between groups of people, and the patterns of power, exclusion and conflict resulting from such differences, become embedded in geographical landscapes. The course examines place-based sites of difference, power, and conflict beginning with the map, and moving through such spatial environments as the body, the city, the nation, the landscape, the reservation, culminating in borderland conflict here in our own backyard.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Topics in Communication
courses.description: Specialized study in communication, with topics to be determined by the instructor for any given quarter.

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Communication Research as an Interdisciplinary Activity
courses.description: A course that introduces students to the interdisciplinary nature of the field of communication research as represented by the work of faculty in the Department of Communication. Through faculty research, students are presented with concrete examples of communication research theory and practice that can provide them with insights for conducting their own research projects.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Directed Group Study
courses.description: The study and analysis of specific topics to be developed by a small group of graduate students under the guidance of an interested faculty member.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Graduate Research
courses.description: Advanced independent study in communication under the guidance of Department of Communication faculty.

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Practice Teaching in Communication
courses.description: A doctoral student in communication is required to assist in teaching undergraduate Department of Communication courses for a total of six quarters. One meeting per week with the instructor, one meeting per week with the assigned sections, and attendance at the lecture of the undergraduate course in which he or she is participating are part of this requirement.

courses.subject: CSS
courses.title: Advanced Programming for Computational Social Science
courses.description: This course develops advanced computational problem-solving skills including common algorithms, data structures, and advanced tool and library options. The class provides further development in Python.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSS 2.

courses.subject: CSS
courses.title: Computational Social Science Research Seminar
courses.description: A weekly seminar series focused on selected topics in computational social science.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing.

courses.subject: CSS
courses.title: Research in Computational Social Science
courses.description: Independent research under the supervision of individual faculty members.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing.

courses.subject: CSS
courses.title: Teaching Apprentice
courses.description: Graduate students are required to enroll in a teaching assistantship course while supporting undergraduate courses.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Principles and Practice of Artificial Intelligence
courses.description: This course introduces students to the conceptual and technological foundations of artificial intelligence (AI) and provides a framework to understand and assess social and ethical aspects of AI. The course will explore the computational basis of intelligence—machine learning (ML) and its various approaches. Students will be exposed to building ML models, training and validating them. The course will delve into how AI is applied and discuss its implications.
courses.prerequisites_text: none. For students to develop a high-level understanding of the AI field. Not for students who plan to study AI, computer science, or data science. Students may only receive credit for one of CSE 5, CSE 5R, or CSE 25.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Programming and Computational Problem-Solving I
courses.description: Introductory course for students interested in computer science and programming. Basics of programming including variables, conditionals, loops, functions/methods. Structured data storage such as arrays/lists and dictionaries, including data mutation. Hands-on experience with designing, writing, hand-tracing, compiling or interpreting, executing, testing, and debugging programs. Students solve relevant computational problems using a high-level programming language. CSE 8A is part of a two-course sequence (CSE 8A-B) that is equivalent to CSE 11. Students should take CSE 8B to complete the CSE 8A/CSE 8B track. Students who have taken CSE 8B or CSE 11 may not take or receive credit for CSE 8A. Students may receive credit for one of the following: COGS 18, CSE 8A, or CSE 6R. Recommended preparation: No prior programming experience is assumed, but comfort using computers is helpful. Students should consult the “CSE Course Placement Advice” web page for assistance in choosing which CSE course to take first.
courses.prerequisites_text: restricted to undergraduates. Graduate students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Programming and Computational Problem-Solving: Accelerated Pace
courses.description: Accelerated introductory programming including an object-oriented approach. Covers basic programming topics from CSE 8A including variables, conditionals, loops, functions/methods, structured data storage, and mutation. Also covers topics from CSE 8B including the Java programming language, class design, interfaces, basic class hierarchies, recursion, event-based programming, and file I/O. Basics of command-line navigation for file management and running programs. Zero units of credit offered for CSE 11 if CSE 8B taken previously or concurrently. Recommended preparation: Significant prior programming experience (for example, high school AP CSA). Students should consult the “CSE Course Placement Advice” web page for assistance in choosing a first CSE course.
courses.prerequisites_text: restricted to undergraduates. Graduate students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Basic Data Structures and Object-Oriented Design
courses.description: Use and implementation of basic data structures including linked lists, stacks, and queues. Use of advanced structures such as binary trees and hash tables. Object-oriented design including interfaces, polymorphism, encapsulation, abstract data types, pre-/post-conditions. Recursion. Uses Java and Java Collections.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 8B or CSE 11; restricted to undergraduates. Graduate students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Discrete Mathematics
courses.description: This course will introduce the ways logic is used in computer science: for reasoning, as a language for specifications, and as operations in computation. Concepts include sets, relations, functions, equivalence relations, partial orders, number systems, and proof methods (especially induction and recursion). Propositional and predicate logic will be introduced and applied to various computer science domains such as circuit design, databases, cryptography, and program correctness. Students who have completed MATH 109 may not receive credit for CSE 20. Credit not offered for both MATH 15A and CSE 20. Equivalent to MATH 15A.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 11 or CSE 6R or CSE 8A or CSE 8B or ECE 15. Prerequisite courses must have been completed with a grade of C– or better; restricted to undergraduates. Graduate students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Mathematics for Algorithms and Systems
courses.description: This course will cover mathematical concepts used to model and analyze algorithms and computer systems. Topics include counting techniques (inclusion-exclusion; recursive counting; permutations and combinations), data representations, analysis of algorithms (order notation; time complexities; loop invariants), recurrence relations, graphs and trees (data structure representations; basic graph algorithms; special classes of graphs), and basic probability and its applications.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 20 or MATH 15A or MATH 31CH; students who have completed MATH 154 or MATH 184 or MATH 188 previously or concurrently may not receive credit for CSE 21; restricted to undergraduates. Graduate students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
courses.description: This course provides a first introduction to artificial intelligence (AI). It covers the definition of AI, the history of AI, the main approaches to AI, and example applications of AI and machine learning (ML). Concepts will be grounded in a range of real-world application projects in AI. Students will also be introduced to ethical issues around AI.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 18 or CSE 11 or CSE 6R or CSE 8A or CSE 8B or DSC 20. Restricted to students within the CS29 major. All other students will be allowed as space permits. This course is intended for students with no prior AI or ML experience. This course is intended for students with no prior AI or ML experience. Students may receive credit for one of the following: CSE 5, CSE 5R, or CSE 25.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Systems Programming and Software Tools
courses.description: A programmer’s view of how computer systems execute programs, store information, and communicate. Emphasis on understanding the details of how a single computer program executes on a computer. Hands-on systems programming using the C programming language and software tools (e.g., gdb, valgrind, make) in the UNIX environment. Builds foundation for courses on computer organization, operating systems, networks, and compilers.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 11 or CSE 8B or ECE 15; two units of credit offered for CSE 29 if CSE 15L taken previously.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Computer Organization
courses.description: Introduction to organization of modern digital computers. Students learn how to write programs in assembly, design basic processors capable of executing the assembly programs, and how to build the basic components of processors using digital logic. Topics include assembly programming, combinational and sequential logic, processor performance, processor design, and the memory hierarchy.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 15L or CSE 29 or ECE 15; restricted to undergraduates. Graduate students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Learning Sustainable Well-Being: Compassion for Self and Others, a Computing Perspective
courses.description: This experiential course teaches the art of practicing psychological well-being, based on Eastern and Western approaches (e.g., mindfulness, positive psychology, cognitive therapy, neuroscience, theatre and art), from a computing perspective. Each week, there is a short lecture on a given topic, combined with workshop-style exercises. (P/NP grades only.)
courses.prerequisites_text: none.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Computer Science and Engineering Seminar
courses.description: A seminar format discussion led by CSE faculty on topics in central areas of computer science, concentrating on the relation among them, recent developments, and future directions. This seminar introduces incoming students to resources and opportunities in the CSE department. May be taken for credit up to three times. Restricted to students in the CSE-PACE program.
courses.prerequisites_text: none.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Tutor Apprenticeship
courses.description: Students assigned to tutor for a CSE course for the first time receive individual and group mentoring and training on how to be effective tutors to help them develop the skills and tools needed to be effective in their tutor role. Students must have a concurrent tutor appointment in a CSE course. See CSE website for application information.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Advanced Data Structures
courses.description: High-performance data structures and supporting algorithms. Use and implementation of data structures like (un)balanced trees, graphs, priority queues, and hash tables. Also memory management, pointers, recursion. Theoretical and practical performance analysis, both average case and amortized. Uses C++ and STL.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 21 or MATH 154 or MATH 158 or MATH 184 or MATH 188 and CSE 12 and CSE 15L or CSE 29 or ECE 15. This course is a distance education course. Students may not receive credit for both CSE 100R and CSE 100.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
courses.description: Design and analysis of efficient algorithms with emphasis of nonnumerical algorithms such as sorting, searching, pattern matching, and graph and network algorithms. Measuring complexity of algorithms, time and storage. NP-complete problems.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 21 or MATH 154 or MATH 158 or MATH 184 or MATH 188 and CSE 12 or DSC 30; restricted to undergraduates. Graduate students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Theory of Computability
courses.description: An introduction to the mathematical theory of computability. Formal languages. Finite automata and regular expressions. Push-down automata and context-free languages. Computable or recursive functions: Turing machines, the halting problem. Undecidability.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 12 and CSE 20 or MATH 109 or MATH 15A or MATH 31CH and CSE 21 or MATH 100A or MATH 103A or MATH 154 or MATH 158 or MATH 184 or MATH 188; restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, EC26, and MA30 majors. Other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Modern Cryptography
courses.description: Topics include private and public-key cryptography, block ciphers, data encryption, authentication, key distribution and certification, pseudorandom number generators, design and analysis of protocols, zero-knowledge proofs, and advanced protocols. Emphasizes rigorous mathematical approach including formal definitions of security goals and proofs of protocol security.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 21 or MATH 154 or MATH 158 or MATH 184 or MATH 188 and CSE 101 and CSE 105; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS28, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Programming Contests
courses.description: This course introduces the algorithms and concepts necessary to compete in programming contests like ACM International Collegiate Programming Contest (ICPC). The course requires weekly completion of short problem sets. Topics covered include standard library classes and data structures useful for programming contest problems, basic complexity analysis, dynamic programming, graph algorithms, number theory, combinatorics, computational geometry, combinatorial games, and contest strategy.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 15L or CSE 29 or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Software Engineering
courses.description: Introduction to software development and engineering methods, including specification, design, implementation, testing, and process. An emphasis on team development, agile methods, and use of tools such as IDE’s, version control, and test harnesses.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 100 or CSE 100R; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Operating Systems Principles
courses.description: Introduces operating systems concepts, including processes, synchronization, scheduling, memory management, virtual memory, file systems, and protection. May be coscheduled with CSE 220.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 15L or CSE 29 and CSE 30 and CSE 100 or CSE 100R and CSE 101; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Computer Networks
courses.description: Introduction to concepts, principles, and practice of computer communication networks with examples from existing architectures, protocols, and standards with special emphasis on internet protocols. Layering and the OSI model; physical and data link layers; local and wide area networks; datagrams and virtual circuits; routing and congestion control; internetworking. Transport protocols. Students may not receive credit for both CSE 123 and ECE 158A.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 15L or CSE 29 and CSE 101 and CSE 110; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, EC26, CS27, CS28, and CS29 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Software System Design and Implementation
courses.description: Design and implementation of large, complex software systems involving multiple aspects of CSE curriculum. Emphasis is on software system design applied to a single, large group project with close interaction with instructor.
courses.prerequisites_text: senior standing with substantial programming experience, and consent of instructor. Department stamp required.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Computer Security
courses.description: Topics include basic cryptography, security/threat analysis, access control, auditing, security models, distributed systems security, and theory behind common attack and defense techniques. The class will go over formal models as well as the bits and bytes of security exploits.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 21 or MATH 154 or MATH 158 or MATH 184 or MATH 188 and CSE 120 or CSE 123 or CSE 124 or ECE 158A or ECE 158B; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS28, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Database System Principles
courses.description: Basic concepts of databases, including data modeling, relational databases, query languages, optimization, dependencies, schema design, and concurrency control. Exposure to one or several commercial database systems. Advanced topics such as deductive and object-oriented databases, time allowing.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 100 or CSE 100R; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, EC26, CS27, CS28, and CS29 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Computer Architecture
courses.description: Introduction to computer architecture. Computer system design. Processor design. Control design. Memory systems. Two units of credit offered for CSE 141 if CSE 142 taken previously.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 30 or ECE 30 and CSE 140; restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Project in Computer Architecture
courses.description: Hands-on computer architecture project aiming to familiarize students with instruction set architecture, and design of process. Control and memory systems.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 30 or ECE 30 and CSE 140; restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, CS28, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Embedded Systems Design Project
courses.description: This project-based course builds an embedded computing system. Topics include rapid system prototyping, hardware/software codesign, technical writing, public speaking, project management, entrepreneurship, and research ethics. May be coscheduled with CSE 237D.
courses.prerequisites_text: instructor approval required, by application only.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence: Probabilistic Reasoning and Decision-Making
courses.description: Introduction to probabilistic models at the heart of modern artificial intelligence. Specific topics to be covered include probabilistic methods for reasoning and decision-making under uncertainty; inference and learning in Bayesian networks; prediction and planning in Markov decision processes; applications to intelligent systems, speech and natural language processing, information retrieval, and robotics.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 12 or DSC 40B and CSE 15L or CSE 29 or DSC 80 and COGS 118D or CSE 103 or ECE 109 or ECON 120A or MAE 108 or MATH 180A or MATH 180B or MATH 181A or MATH 183 or MATH 186 and MATH 20A and MATH 18 or MATH 31AH; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, EC26, and DS25 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence: Search and Reasoning
courses.description: The course will introduce important ideas and algorithms in search and reasoning and demonstrate how they are used in practical AI applications. Topics include A* search, adversarial search, Monte Carlo tree search, reinforcement learning, constraint solving and optimization, propositional and first-order reasoning.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 12 or DSC 40B and CSE 15L or CSE 29 or DSC 80 and COGS 118D or CSE 103 or ECE 109 or ECON 120A or MAE 108 or MATH 180A or MATH 180B or MATH 181A or MATH 183 or MATH 186 and CSE 100 or CSE 100R; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, EC26, and DS25 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Machine Learning: Learning Algorithms
courses.description: Broad introduction to machine learning. The topics include some topics in supervised learning, such as k-nearest neighbor classifiers, decision trees, boosting, and perceptrons; and topics in unsupervised learning, such as k-means and hierarchical clustering. In addition to the actual algorithms, the course focuses on the principles behind the algorithms. Students may not receive credit for both CSE 151A and COGS 188. May be coscheduled with CSE 251A.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 12 or DSC 40B and CSE 15L or CSE 29 or DSC 80 and COGS 118D or CSE 103 or ECE 109 or ECON 120A or MAE 108 or MATH 180A or MATH 180B or MATH 181A or MATH 183 or MATH 186 and MATH 18 or MATH 31AH and MATH 20C or MATH 31BH; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, EC26, and DS25 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Deep Learning
courses.description: This course covers the fundamentals of deep neural networks at the undergraduate level. We introduce linear regression, multi-layer perceptrons, backpropagation, and automatic differentiation. We will also discuss convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and transformers. The course will be a combination of lectures, presentations, and machine learning competitions. Renumbered from CSE 154. Students may receive credit for one of the following: CSE 151B, CSE 154, or COGS 181. May be coscheduled with CSE 251B. Recommended preparation: knowledge of Python.
courses.prerequisites_text: MATH 20C or MATH 31BH and BENG 134 or COGS 118D or CSE 103 or ECE 109 or ECON 120A or MAE 108 or MATH 180A or MATH 180B or MATH 181A or MATH 183 or MATH 186 or SE 125 and COGS 118A or COGS 118B or COGS 188 or CSE 151A or DSC 140B or ECE 175A; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS28, CS29, EC26, and DS25 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Computer Vision I
courses.description: This course provides a broad introduction to the foundations, algorithms, and applications of computer vision. It introduces classical models and contemporary methods, from image formation models to deep learning, to address problems of 3-D reconstruction and object recognition from images and video. Topics include filtering, feature detection, stereo vision, structure from motion, motion estimation, and recognition. Programming assignments will be in Python. Students may not receive credit for both CSE 152A and CSE 152.
courses.prerequisites_text: MATH 18 or MATH 31AH and CSE 12 or DSC 30 and CSE 15L or CSE 29 or DSC 80; Python programming experience recommended; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Machine Learning for Music
courses.description: This course will introduce students to the application of machine learning to understand and generate music. The course will cover data structures for music representation; predictive tasks and music information retrieval; and techniques for algorithmic music synthesis. May be coscheduled with CSE 253. Students may not receive credit for CSE 153 and CSE 153R.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 12 or DSC 40B and CSE 15L or CSE 29 or DSC 80 and BENG 100 or BENG 134 or COGS 118D or CSE 103 or ECE 109 or ECON 120A or MAE 108 or MATH 180A or MATH 180B or MATH 181A or MATH 183 or MATH 186; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS28, CS29, EC26, and DS25 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Machine Learning for Music
courses.description: This course will introduce students to the application of machine learning to understand and generate music. The course will cover data structures for music representation; predictive tasks and music information retrieval; and techniques for algorithmic music synthesis. This is a distance education course. May be coscheduled with CSE 253. Students may not receive credit for CSE 153R and CSE 153.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 12 or DSC 40B and CSE 15L or CSE 29 or DSC 80 and BENG 100 or BENG 134 or COGS 118D or CSE 103 or ECE 109 or ECON 120A or MAE 108 or MATH 180A or MATH 180B or MATH 181A or MATH 183 or MATH 186; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS28, CS29, EC26, and DS25 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: 3-D User Interaction
courses.description: This course focuses on the design of three-dimensional (3-D) user interfaces, VR devices, and interaction techniques. The course consists of lectures, student presentations, and programming assignments. Students will be expected to create VR applications to learn how VR displays and 3-D interactions work.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 167 or CSE 167R or MATH 155A; restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Image Processing
courses.description: Principles of image formation, analysis, and representation. Image enhancement, restoration, and segmentation; stochastic image models. Filter design, sampling, Fourier and wavelet transforms. Selected applications in computer graphics and machine vision.
courses.prerequisites_text: DSC 40B or MATH 18 or MATH 31AH and CSE 100 or CSE 100R or DSC 80.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Computer Graphics II: Rendering
courses.description: Weekly programming assignments that will cover graphics rendering algorithms. During the course the students will learn about ray tracing, geometry, tessellation, acceleration structures, sampling, filtering, shading models, and advanced topics such as global illumination and programmable graphics hardware. Students may not receive credit for CSE 168 and CSE 168R.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 167 or CSE 167R or MATH 155A; restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Successful Entrepreneurship for Engineers
courses.description: A foundation course teaching the basics of starting and running a successful new business. Students learn how to think like entrepreneurs, pivot their ideas to match customer needs, with financial, market, timeline feasibility inputs. The end goal is an investor pitch and a business plan. Provides experiential education, encouragement, and coaching (E3CE) that prepares students for successful careers at start-up as well as large companies.
courses.prerequisites_text: instructor approval required to ensure sufficient project experience to be successful in the course. No credit offered for CSE 175 if ECE 150 taken previously or concurrently.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Biological Databases
courses.description: This course provides an introduction to the features of biological data, how those data are organized efficiently in databases, and how existing data resources can be utilized to solve a variety of biological problems. Object oriented databases, data modeling and description. Survey of current biological database with respect to above, implementation of a database on a biological topic. Students may receive credit for one of the following: CSE 182, BENG 182, or BIMM 182.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 100 or CSE 100R; restricted to BE28, BI34, CH37, and CS27 majors.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Advanced Bioinformatics Laboratory
courses.description: This course emphasizes the hands-on application of bioinformatics to biological problems. Students will gain experience in the application of existing software, as well as in combining approaches to answer specific biological questions. Topics include sequence alignment, fast database search, comparative genomics, expression analysis, computational proteomics, genome-wide association studies, next-generation sequencing, genomics, and big data. Students may not receive credit for CSE 185 and BIMM 185. Restricted to CS27, BI34, BE28, and CH37 majors.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 11 or CSE 8B and CSE 12 and MATH 20C or MATH 31BH and BILD 1 and BIEB 123 or BILD 4 or BIMM 101 or CHEM 109.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Topics in Computer Science and Engineering
courses.description: Topics of special interest in computer science and engineering. Topics may vary from quarter to quarter. May be repeated for credit with the consent of instructor. May be taken for credit up to three times. May be coscheduled with CSE 291.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor. Department stamp required.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Seminar in CSE
courses.description: A seminar course on topics of current interest. Students, as well as the instructor, will be actively involved in running the course/class. This course cannot be counted toward a technical elective.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor. Department stamp required.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Field Study in Computer Science and Engineering
courses.description: Directed study accompanying full-time on-site computer science internships. (P/NP grades only.)
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of the instructor and approval of the department required. Students may receive credit for one of the following: CSE 197 or CSE 197C. Restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, and CS29 majors only.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Directed Group Study
courses.description: Computer science and engineering topics whose study involves reading and discussion by a small group of students under the supervision of a faculty member. (P/NP grades only.)
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of the instructor. Department stamp required.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Independent Study for Undergraduates
courses.description: Independent reading or research by special arrangement with a faculty member. (P/NP grades only.)
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of the instructor. Department stamp required.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: CSE Honors Thesis Research for Undergraduates
courses.description: Undergraduate research for completing an honors project under the supervision of a CSE faculty member. May be taken across multiple quarters. Students should enroll for a letter grade. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: Admission to the CSE department honors program. Consent of the instructor. Department stamp required.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Computability and Complexity
courses.description: Computability review, including halting problem, decidable sets, r.e. sets, many-one reductions; TIME(t(n)), SPACE(s(n)) and general relations between these classes; L, P, PSPACE, NP; NP—completeness; hierarchy theorems; RP, BPP.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 105 or equivalent.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Advanced Algorithms
courses.description: Modern advances in design and analysis of algorithms. Exact syllabus varies. Topics include approximation, randomized algorithms, probabilistic analysis, heuristics, online algorithms, competitive analysis, models of memory hierarchy, parallel algorithms, number-theoretic algorithms, cryptanalysis, computational geometry, computational biology, network algorithms, VLSI CAD algorithms.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 202.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Advanced Cryptography
courses.description: Zero-knowledge, secure computation, session-key distribution, protocols, electronic payment, one-way functions, trapdoor permutations, pseudorandom bit generators, hardcore bits.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 202, CSE 200, and CSE 207 or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Topics/Seminar in Algorithms, Complexity, and Logic
courses.description: Topics of special interest in algorithms, complexity, and logic to be presented by faculty and students under faculty direction. Topics vary from quarter to quarter. May be repeated for credit.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Human-Centered Computing for Health (HC4H)
courses.description: This interdisciplinary course brings together students from engineering, design, and medicine, and exposes them to designing technology for health and health care. The course is focused on studying how technology is used in health care and identifies opportunities for novel technology to be developed for specific health and health-care settings. Students will be exposed to the health domain at large through site visits and discussions with experts in a variety of health-care domains. Site visits will be coordinated by the department.
courses.prerequisites_text: department approval and instructor consent required.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Design at Large
courses.description: New societal challenges, cultural values, and technological opportunities are changing design—and vice versa. The seminar explores this increased scale, real-world engagement, and disruptive impact. Invited speakers from UC San Diego and beyond share cutting-edge research on interaction, design, and learning. Cross-listed with COGS 229. (S/U grades only.)
courses.prerequisites_text: none.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Distributed Computing and Systems
courses.description: Efficient primitives for distributed operating systems and high-performance network servers, including concurrent and event-driven server architectures, remote procedure calls, and load shedding. Distributed naming, directory, and storage services, replication for fault tolerance, and security in distributed systems.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 221, CSE 222A, or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Computer Security
courses.description: Security and threat models, risk analysis, authentication and authorization, auditing, operating systems security, access control mechanisms, protection mechanisms, distributed systems/network security, security architecture, electronic commerce security mechanisms, security evaluation.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 221 or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Topics/Seminar in Computer Systems
courses.description: Discussion on problems of current research interest in computer systems. Possible areas of focus include distributed computing, computational grid, operating systems, fault-tolerant computing, storage systems, system services for the World Wide Web. Topics to be presented by faculty and students under faculty direction. Topics vary from quarter to quarter. May be repeated for credit.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Topics/Seminar in Computer Security
courses.description: Discussion on problems of current research interest in computer security. Topics to be presented by faculty and students under faculty direction. Topics vary from quarter to quarter. May be repeated for credit.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Principles of Programming Languages
courses.description: (Formerly CSE 273.) Functional versus imperative programming. Type systems and polymorphism; the ML language. Higher order functions, lazy evaluation. Abstract versus concrete syntax, structural and well-founded induction. The lambda calculus, reduction strategies, combinators. Denotational semantics, elementary domain theory. Restricted to students within the CS75, CS78, CS89, CS88, CS77, CS80, CS81, CS83, and CS76 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Compiler Construction
courses.description: (Formerly CSE 264C.) Advanced material in programming languages and translator systems. Topics include compilers and code optimization. May be coscheduled with CSE 131.
courses.prerequisites_text: restricted to students within the CS75, CS76, CS78, CS88, and CS89 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Principles of Database Systems
courses.description: (Formerly CSE 264D.) Database models including relational, hierarchic, and network approaches. Implementation of databases including query languages and system architectures. Restricted to students within the CS75, CS78, CS89, CS88, CS77, CS80, CS81, CS83, and CS76 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Database System Implementation
courses.description: A hands-on approach to the principles of databases implementation. Algebraic rewriters/optimizers, query processors, triggers. Beyond centralized relational databases.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 232.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Embedded Systems Design Project
courses.description: This project-based course builds an embedded computing system. Topics include rapid system prototyping, hardware/software codesign, technical writing, public speaking, project management, entrepreneurship, and research ethics. May be coscheduled with CSE 145.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Topics/Seminar in Databases
courses.description: Discussion on problems of current research interest in databases. Possible areas of focus include core database issues, data management on the web, data integration, new database models and applications, formal methods in databases. Topics to be presented by faculty and students under faculty direction. Topics vary from quarter to quarter. May be repeated for credit.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Topics/Seminar in Programming Languages
courses.description: Discussion on problems of current research interest in programming languages, formal methods, and software engineering. Possible areas of focus include program verification, program synthesis, language design and implementation, developer productivity tools, language-based security. Topics to be presented by faculty and students under faculty direction. Topics vary from quarter to quarter. May be taken for credit up to eighteen times for a maximum of eighteen units.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: VLSI Integration of Computing Circuitry
courses.description: VLSI integrated-circuit building blocks of computing systems, and their implementation. Computer-aided design and performance simulations, design exercises and projects. Devices, standard cells and interconnects, clocking, power/ground distribution, arithmetic modules, memories. Methodologies and tradeoffs in system implementation.
courses.prerequisites_text: layout (CSE 165 or ECE 260A) and logic design (CSE 140 or ECE 111), or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Seminar in Embedded Systems
courses.description: Topics of special interest to researchers in embedded systems and mobile computing to be presented by faculty and students under faculty direction. Topics vary from quarter to quarter. Representative work usually found at venues such as CPS-IOT Week, SenSys, MobiCom, MobiSys, ESWEEK, and IMWUT (UbiComp). May be taken up to twenty-four times for credit.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Deep Learning
courses.description: (Formerly CSE 253.) This course covers the fundamentals of deep neural networks at the graduate level. We introduce multi-layer perceptrons, backpropagation, and automatic differentiation. We will also discuss convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, transformers, and advanced topics in deep learning. The course will be a combination of lectures, presentations, and machine learning competitions. Renumbered from CSE 253. Students may not receive credit for CSE 251B and CSE 253. Course may be coscheduled with CSE 151B. Recommended preparation: knowledge of Python.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 251A. Restricted to students within the CS75, CS76, CS78, CS88, and CS89 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Advanced Computer Vision
courses.description: This course covers advanced concepts in computer vision. Example topics include 3-D reconstruction, face recognition, object detection, semantic segmentation, action recognition, and domain adaptation. Consistent with recent developments, deep learning forms a significant fraction of the class. Lectures and assignments cover recent works on fundamental problems in computer vision, with the aim to prepare students for pursuing careers in the field. Recommended preparation: Completion of one of CSE 252A, 252B, 250A, or 250B is highly recommended.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Machine Learning for Music
courses.description: This course will introduce students to the application of machine learning to understand and generate music.
